summary: For ages 6-8, pictograms, tally charts, block diagrams and simple tables are the first formal data representations: each turns counts into a picture (or table) and back again. Learners should both read a given chart (what does this tell us? how many?) and construct one from data they collected. The load-bearing ideas are the tally's grouping in gated fives, the pictogram's key (one symbol standing for one, later for several), and a block diagram's equal, aligned blocks on a common baseline so that height/length means count. Move deliberately between picture and numbers in both directions.
misconceptions: Reads each pictogram symbol as 'one' when the key says it stands for several (ignores the key / many-to-one)
Counts tally marks one-by-one and miscounts, or draws the fifth mark as a fifth upright instead of the diagonal gate
Misreads a block diagram or pictogram by length when blocks/symbols are unequal or not aligned to a baseline
Constructs a chart with uneven gaps, unequal symbols, or no key, so it cannot be read back accurately

activities.title: Two-way chart builder from the class's own data
steps: Collect or be given a stream of survey results (e.g. favourite pets) and record them as tally marks, forming gated fives (four uprights with a diagonal fifth) and counting in fives
Also record the counts in a simple table linking each category to its frequency
Stamp or draw pictogram symbols into aligned rows next to an explicit key, reading the key first: 'one picture = one child'
Answer read-back questions such as 'how many children chose dogs?' and check against the highlighted row
Flip the key to 'one picture = 2' and re-state what the same row now means, then construct a new row from a given count under that key
Rebuild the data as a block diagram with equal-sized blocks aligned to a common baseline
activities.insight: A chart or table is a reversible translation between counts and a picture; the key governs what each symbol is worth, and height/length can only be trusted when units are equal and aligned to a baseline.

activities.title: Many-to-one key: read through it and reverse it
steps: Read a pictogram whose key says one picture stands for 2 pets, and state how many children have a dog, explaining how the key was used
Interpret a half-symbol under the key: say how many it represents and justify your answer
Reverse the direction: given a tally showing 6 fish, draw the pictogram row using the same key, deciding how many whole symbols are needed
Given that existing fish row, show how it would change if 3 more fish joined, keeping to the same key
Compare a pictogram where one symbol means one individual with a pictogram where one symbol stands for several, and say which key is in use
activities.insight: The key must be applied, not assumed: a many-to-one pictogram is read as symbols times the key value, and constructing a row reverses that (6 fish become 3 symbols under a key of 2); updating a count means changing the number of symbols by the added count divided by the key value (3 more fish under a key of 2 means 1½ more symbols, so 9 fish = 4½ symbols).

activities.title: Check for value-by-length and tally errors
steps: Look at a block diagram or pictogram where blocks/symbols are unequal or off the baseline and decide whether the longest row really is 'most', stating what you would check
Count a set of tally marks that includes ungated or slow one-by-one groups and recount using gated fives
Add a new category to an existing chart and check the chart can still be read back accurately
activities.insight: Height or length means count only when units are equal and aligned to a common baseline; tallies are counted reliably in gated fives, not one by one.

checkQuestion: First: here is a pictogram of our class's pets with a key saying one picture stands for 2 pets — how many children have a dog, and how did you work it out? Then: here is the tally for fish, showing 6 — draw the pictogram row for fish using the same key.
checkAnswer: Interpreting: uses the key (counts the dog symbols and multiplies by 2, halving for any half-symbol) to state the correct frequency and explains the key was used. Translating: draws 3 whole symbols for 6 fish (because each = 2), aligned in the row — showing the key works both directions.
